title: Stage occupancy sankey and quantile synopsis (p50/p95/p99)
body:
Purpose:
This note captures a compact, pragmatic view of end-to-end emission latency by combining stage occupancy metrics with quantile timing (p50/p95/p99). The goal is to expose where time is spent as load shifts so we can prioritize inexpensive mitigations (batching tweaks, cache pre-warm, serialization hotpath) versus heavier work (model kernel tuning, hardware mapping).

Dataset and method:
- Sampled ~30k successful responses over a 6-hour evening window (US-East peak).
- Traces were annotated with stage boundaries: ingest -> deserialize -> preprocess -> tokenize -> batching_wait -> model_forward -> kv_lookup -> postprocess -> serialize -> egress.
- Occupancy measurement: wall-clock time each request spent in a given stage across its lifecycle (includes queue wait inside that stage).
- Quantiles computed across same sample slice; stage times sum per trace approximately equals end-to-end duration (small variance due to concurrent bookkeeping).
- Sankey visualization was generated from aggregated stage occupancy fractions for p50/p95/p99 cohorts to show shifting dominances.

High-level numbers (end-to-end):
- p50 overall: 82 ms
- p95 overall: 210 ms
- p99 overall: 420 ms

Representative per-stage quantiles (ms) - median / p95 / p99 (stage order approximates critical path):
- ingest: 4 / 9 / 14
- deserialize: 3 / 7 / 12
- preprocess: 9 / 18 / 30
- tokenize: 2 / 6 / 10
- batching_wait: 10 / 35 / 90
- model_forward: 38 / 120 / 280
- kv_lookup: 6 / 15 / 36
- postprocess: 7 / 14 / 26
- serialize: 2 / 4 / 7
- egress: 1 / 2 / 4

Notes on numbers and shape:
- model_forward dominates p50-to-p99 growth in absolute terms but batching_wait is the most volatile contributor to p95 spikes: its p99 (90 ms) amplifies shorter sequences where model_forward is small.
- kv_lookup p99 (36 ms) correlates tightly with traces where a cache miss triggers a slow fallback to remote datastore. Those traces also show increased deserialize and serialize time (payloads larger).
- The sankey for p50 shows model_forward ~46% of occupancy, batching_wait ~12%, remaining stages split small. For p99 the sankey shifts: model_forward ~66%, batching_wait ~21%, kv/fallback ~8% combined.
- We observed two dominant trace archetypes: (A) long model runs (larger sequences / sampling steps) where model_forward alone explains >75% of end-to-end; (B) short model runs with high wait or cache misses where batching_wait + kv_lookup together push p95/p99.

Root-cause signals and heuristics applied during triage:
- Queue depth and batch formation: when QPS spikes by >2x the batching policy increases typical batching_wait by 2–4x due to conservative timeout; also exacerbated by skewed arrival patterns (bursty clients).
- KV cache TTL and coldness: certain keys (customer-specific prompt templates) have TTLs misaligned with traffic, causing elevated miss rates on a small but high-impact cohort. Misses introduce 20–60ms variance depending on remote datastore latency.
- Model stepping and kernel selection: p99 traces for model_forward often show degraded kernel selection metrics (fallback to slower matmul kernel under certain sequence length combos).
- Serialization path: large payload branches (structured tool outputs) show extra deserialize/serialize time; these are responsible for ~3–8% of p99 tail in traces with >2KB payloads.

Actionable mitigations (cheap first):
- Reduce batching timeout floor for routes with sub-100ms model_forward median and strong burstiness: test lowered floor from 8ms -> 4ms and monitor p95 change for short-seqlen cohort.
- Add small in-memory LRU for templated prompt keys to reduce kv miss fraction (target top 2% of keys by frequency).
- Introduce an early-exit path for tiny payloads to bypass full deserialize/serialize for known compact formats.
- Warm model kernels for common seqlen buckets during autoscale events to avoid slow kernel fallback.

Longer-term/engineering projects:
- Adaptive batching policy: dynamic floor based on observed arrival entropy (burstiness metric) to minimize batching_wait tail without sacrificing throughput.
- Route-aware caching: per-customer small LRU + async background refresh for recently evicted hot keys.
- Kernel/compilation profiling harness: systematic offline runner to detect sequence-length -> kernel-degradation points and produce precompiled kernels.

Validation windows and success criteria:
- Short-term experiments (A/B) should run for at least 48h across two peak windows. Success criteria: p95 drop >= 15% for short-seqlen cohort and no >5% throughput regression.
- KV LRU pilot: reduce observed cache-miss p99 contribution by 40% on targeted keys and total p99 by >=6 ms.

Open questions / unknowns to address in follow-ups:
- Precise mapping between kernel fallback signals and per-trace metadata (we have a noisy signal from runtime logs; need stronger correlation keys).
- Whether any multi-tenant interference on hardware is contributing to sporadic model_forward p99 spikes (requires dedicated capacity experiment).
- Impact of client-side retry patterns that may artificially increase batching_wait under certain SLA configs.

Appendix: quick trace archetype examples (anonymized):
- Archetype A (long-run): end-to-end 760 ms (p99-like); stage breakdown: model_forward 520 ms, batching_wait 40 ms, kv_lookup 20 ms, others 180 ms. Notes: large seqlen, kernel fallback observed.
- Archetype B (short-run, missy): end-to-end 380 ms; stage breakdown: model_forward 60 ms, batching_wait 120 ms, kv_lookup 36 ms, deserialize/serialize 30 ms, others 134 ms. Notes: cache miss + bursty arrival.

Concluding summary:
Combining occupancy fractions with quantile timing gives an interpretable view of how tail behavior emerges: for our workload, model compute is the largest single contributor to tails, but queue/batching dynamics and cache misses are multiplicative pain points for shorter requests. The recommended first experiments (batching floor adjustments + small-key LRU) are low-effort and target the most actionable tail drivers observed in the dataset.

If reviewers want the sankey visuals and per-trace CSVs, see linked artifacts and the PR for the viz generation.
next_steps: Create A/B branch to test batching timeout floor change (8ms -> 4ms) for route: chat-small-seq
Prototype in-memory LRU for templated prompts and run pilot on 10% of traffic
Add stronger kernel fallback logging correlation IDs to runtime traces
Schedule dedicated-capacity 2-hour run to rule out hardware multi-tenant interference
